title: PHY_108 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: In every PHY_108 experiment one measured quantity is placed on the horizontal axis. Which quantity is it?
options: The quantity with the larger numerical values
The quantity measured with the more precise instrument
The quantity the experimenter sets or controls
The quantity whose unit is an SI base unit
questions.why: Why C is right: The horizontal axis carries the independent variable — the thing you choose and step (time in the RC experiments, mass in the Young's modulus experiment, distance d in the bar-magnet experiment). The dependent variable, the one you read off an instrument in response, goes on the vertical axis. Why the others are wrong: A chooses the axis by size of the numbers, which is a scaling matter, not a role · B confuses precision of the instrument with the independent/dependent distinction · D invents a rule about units that has nothing to do with which variable is controlled

questions.q: A straight line passes through the points (0, −1) and (4, −3). What is its x-intercept?
questions.why: Why A is right: m = (−3 − (−1))/(4 − 0) = −2/4 = −0.50, and the point (0, −1) gives c = −1.00. x-intercept = −c/m = −(−1.00)/(−0.50) = −2.00. Why the others are wrong: B drops one of the two minus signs in −c/m · C inverts the slope, using (x₂−x₁)/(y₂−y₁) = −2, then −c/m = −0.50 · D inverts the slope and loses a sign as well

questions.q: The line 7y − 40x = 35 is rewritten in the form y = mx + c. What is the value of c?
questions.why: Why D is right: 7y = 40x + 35, so y = (40/7)x + 5. The y-intercept is 5.00 and the slope is 40/7 = 5.71. Why the others are wrong: A reads the constant off before dividing the whole equation by 7 · B quotes the slope 40/7 in place of the intercept · C carries the sign across the equals sign twice

questions.q: For a simple pendulum, T² is plotted against L and the best-fit line has a slope of 4.02 s²/m. What value of g does this give?
questions.why: Why B is right: T = 2π√(L/g) linearises to T² = (4π²/g)L, so slope = 4π²/g and g = 4π²/slope = 39.478/4.02 = 9.82 m/s². Why the others are wrong: A inverts the relation, computing slope/4π² instead of 4π²/slope · C quotes 4π² itself and never divides by the slope · D uses 4π instead of 4π² in the numerator

questions.q: Why is T² plotted against L for a simple pendulum rather than T against L?
options: Because T² is proportional to L, so the plot is straight and its gradient carries g
Because squaring the period removes the random error in the timing
Because T against L is also straight, but its gradient has no physical meaning
Because squaring converts the period into SI units
questions.why: Why A is right: Linearisation exists so that a constant can be read with a ruler from all the points at once. T against L is a curve; T² against L is straight, with gradient 4π²/g. Why the others are wrong: B confuses an algebraic transformation with error reduction; squaring does not cancel scatter · C wrongly claims T against L is linear · D seconds are already SI; squaring changes the quantity, not the unit system

questions.q: Radioactive decay follows N = N₀e^(−λt). Which plot gives a straight line, and what is its slope?
options: ln N against ln t; slope = −λ
ln N against t; slope = +λ
N against ln t; slope = −1/λ
ln N against t; slope = −λ
questions.why: Why D is right: Taking natural logs, ln N = −λt + ln N₀. Only the y-quantity is logged; time stays linear. The slope is −λ and the intercept is ln N₀. Why the others are wrong: A applies the power-law rule (log both axes) to an exponential, where only y is logged · B loses the minus sign, so a decay constant comes out negative · C logs the wrong axis and inverts the constant as well

questions.q: For a power law y = kxⁿ, log₁₀ y is plotted against log₁₀ x. The intercept is 0.60. What is k?
questions.why: Why B is right: log y = n log x + log k, so the intercept is log₁₀ k = 0.60 and k = 10^0.60 = 3.98. Why the others are wrong: A reads the intercept itself as k, forgetting it is a logarithm · C uses e^0.60, mixing natural logs into a base-10 plot · D takes the reciprocal, 1/10^0.60

questions.q: A gas sample is tested by plotting log P against log V. The points lie on a good straight line of slope −1.4. What does this show?
options: Boyle's law holds and the constant k is equal to 1.4
The axes have been interchanged; the true slope is −1
The sample does not obey Boyle's law over that range
The volumes were recorded in millilitres instead of cubic metres
questions.why: Why C is right: Boyle's law, PV = k, linearises to log P = −log V + log k, so the slope must be −1. A straight line of slope −1.4 means the points follow some power law, but not the one Boyle's law predicts. Why the others are wrong: A reads the slope as the constant; k comes from the intercept, not the gradient · B interchanging log P and log V would give −1/1.4 = −0.71, not −1 · D a unit change shifts the intercept only; it cannot change the slope of a log-log plot

questions.q: Coulomb's law is F = kq₁q₂/r². To obtain a straight line through the origin, what should be plotted, and what does the slope equal?
options: F against r²; slope = kq₁q₂
F against 1/r; slope = kq₁q₂
1/F against r²; slope = kq₁q₂
F against 1/r²; slope = kq₁q₂
questions.why: Why D is right: Writing F = (kq₁q₂)(1/r²) matches y = mx + c with y = F, x = 1/r², m = kq₁q₂ and c = 0. Why the others are wrong: A forgets to take the reciprocal, so the plot is a curve · B takes the reciprocal but drops the square · C inverts both variables, which is linear but has slope 1/(kq₁q₂), not kq₁q₂

questions.q: Why must each axis of a laboratory graph carry the unit as well as the name of the quantity?
options: Because unlabelled axes make the graph harder for a reader to follow and to check afterwards
Because the slope's unit is (unit of y)/(unit of x), without which it cannot become a physical quantity
Because the intercept can only be located once the axes carry units
Because the units confirm that the scale is 1, 2, 5 or 10 units per square
questions.why: Why B is right: A slope of 0.998 read from unlabelled axes is a bare number. Only the units tell you it is 0.998 V/mA, and therefore 998 Ω rather than 0.998 Ω. Why the others are wrong: A gives a presentational reason for what is actually an analytical necessity · C the intercept is read from the scale; units are needed to interpret it, not to find it · D confuses labelling with scaling; the two rules are independent

questions.q: Why should a best-fit line not be drawn so that it passes through every plotted point?
options: Because a line through every point would have to be curved, and curves cannot be used
Because the first and last points are the most reliable and should define the line
Because the scatter of the points is random error, and the line exists to average it out
Because a point that lies off the line is a blunder and should be deleted
questions.why: Why C is right: A graph is an averaging device. Joining the dots preserves exactly the scatter the line was drawn to remove, and the resulting 'curve' is invented physics. Why the others are wrong: A curves are legitimate results; the objection is to preserving random scatter · B forcing the line through the end points is itself a listed mistake · D an outlier is plotted, ignored when drawing the line and commented on, never quietly removed

questions.q: From which two points should the slope of a graph be measured?
options: Two widely separated points that lie on the drawn best-fit line
The first and last plotted data points
Two adjacent data points near the middle of the run
The two data points that lie furthest from the line
questions.why: Why A is right: The points must lie on the line, because data points sit off it and reintroduce the scatter the line removed; and they must be far apart, so the reading error is a small fraction of the triangle. Why the others are wrong: B uses raw data rather than the line — the commonest and costliest slope error · C uses raw data and a small triangle, magnifying the reading error · D deliberately picks the worst points, maximising the scatter carried into the slope

questions.q: Two points taken from a best-fit line are 5.00 mA apart along the current axis. Each current is read to ±0.02 mA. What percentage of the run does that reading error represent?
questions.why: Why B is right: (0.02/5.00) × 100 = 0.4 %. Choosing a large triangle is what makes the fractional uncertainty in the slope small; over a run of only 0.50 mA the same error would be 4 %. Why the others are wrong: A uses a run of 0.50 mA — the small-triangle case the rule is designed to avoid · C loses a factor of ten in the multiplication by 100 · D computes the fraction 0.02/5.00 and labels it a percentage without multiplying by 100

questions.q: When should the origin (0, 0) be included on the axes of a PHY_108 graph?
options: Always, because every graph must show where both quantities are zero
Only when one of the variables takes negative values
When the intercept is needed, or when theory says the line passes through it
Never, because including it compresses the data into one corner
questions.why: Why C is right: The origin is not compulsory. Week 2 and Week 12 include it because 'passes through the origin' is part of what is being verified; elsewhere excluding it lets the points fill the grid. Why the others are wrong: A wastes the grid and throws away precision when the data lie far from zero · B negative values require the axis to extend, not the origin to be shown · D would prevent the origin test that verifies Ohm's law and Hooke's law ### Section B — Error, uncertainty and percentage error (Week 1)

questions.q: In practical physics, error is defined as:
options: The difference between a measured value and the true value
A mistake made by the experimenter while taking a reading
The range over which repeated readings scatter
The difference between two successive measurements of the same quantity
questions.why: Why A is right: That is the definition to write verbatim. An error is not a mistake: dropping the thermometer is a blunder, while an error is the unavoidable gap between a reading and the truth. Why the others are wrong: B confuses a blunder with an error; blunders are not part of error analysis · C describes the spread of readings, which is one symptom of random error only · D compares two readings with each other rather than with the true value

questions.q: A measurement is repeated eight times and the readings are averaged. What does this achieve?
options: It reduces both the random and the systematic error
It reduces the systematic error but not the random error
It eliminates both, provided enough readings are taken
It reduces the random error but leaves the systematic error untouched
questions.why: Why D is right: Random errors push readings both ways about the true value, so they partly cancel on averaging. A systematic error shifts every reading the same way by the same amount, so the mean is shifted too. Why the others are wrong: A assumes averaging cures a consistent instrument fault, which it cannot · B reverses the two categories completely · C no number of repeats removes a zero offset, and random error is only reduced, never eliminated

questions.q: A voltmeter reads 0.1 V high on every reading. What effect does this have on the V against I graph?
options: The whole line is displaced, so the intercept is wrong while the slope is unaffected
The points scatter about the line more widely than they otherwise would have done
The line becomes curved
The slope is wrong but the intercept is unaffected
questions.why: Why A is right: A constant offset adds the same amount to every y-value, translating the line vertically. The gradient — the difference between points — is unchanged. This is why the course extracts physics from slopes rather than single readings. Why the others are wrong: B describes random error; a consistent offset produces no extra scatter · C a constant offset is a translation, not a distortion of shape · D reverses which of the two the offset corrupts

questions.q: A man measures a rope as 6.0 m when its true length is 6.3 m. What is the percentage error?
questions.why: Why C is right: Actual error = |6.3 − 6.0| = 0.3 m. Percentage error = (0.3/6.3) × 100 = 4.76 %, which is 4.8 % to two significant figures. The denominator is always the true value. Why the others are wrong: A divides by the measured value 6.0 instead of the true value 6.3 · B computes the fraction 0.0476 and then labels it a percentage without multiplying by 100 · D quotes the absolute error in metres as though it were a percentage

questions.q: A stopwatch gives 12.4 s for an interval whose true duration is 12.0 s. What is the relative (fractional) error?
questions.why: Why B is right: Relative error = actual error / true value = 0.4/12.0 = 0.0333. It is a pure ratio; multiplying by 100 would turn it into the percentage error, 3.33 %. Why the others are wrong: A divides by the measured 12.4 rather than the true 12.0 · C quotes the percentage while the question asks for the fraction · D gives the actual error in seconds instead of the ratio

questions.q: A voltmeter reads 4.9873 V every time it is used, when the true potential difference is 5.40 V. The instrument is best described as:
options: Accurate but not precise, with a random error
Both precise and accurate, since the reading has five significant figures
Neither precise nor accurate, because of large random error
Precise but not accurate, with a systematic error
questions.why: Why D is right: Repeatability is precision; closeness to the truth is accuracy. A consistent offset leaves precision perfect while destroying accuracy — the most dangerous combination, because the readings look trustworthy. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two terms; the readings are reproducible, not scattered · B treats the number of digits displayed as evidence of correctness · C there is no scatter at all in the readings described

questions.q: A calculated result R is proportional to the cube of a measured length d. The length is measured with a fractional uncertainty of 0.8 %. What fractional uncertainty does this contribute to R?
questions.why: Why D is right: For a power, the fractional error is multiplied by the power: ΔR/R ≈ 3 × Δd/d = 3 × 0.8 % = 2.4 %. This is exactly why the thickness of the beam in Week 12 must be measured most carefully. Why the others are wrong: A ignores the power altogether and passes the uncertainty through unchanged · B treats d as squared rather than cubed · C divides by the power instead of multiplying by it

questions.q: Which of the following is a systematic error?
options: A metre rule whose zero end has been worn away
The last digit of a digital meter fluctuating between readings
Viewing the scale from a slightly different angle each time
Variation in the observer's reaction time on a stopwatch
questions.why: Why A is right: A worn zero shifts every length reading by the same amount in the same direction — the definition of a systematic error, caused by a consistent failure of the instrument. Why the others are wrong: B unpredictable fluctuation is random error, reduced by averaging · C varying parallax scatters readings both ways, so it is random · D reaction time varies from trial to trial, so its effect is random ### Section C — Ohm's law and resistor networks (Week 2)

questions.q: Why is the ammeter connected in series with the resistor and given a very low resistance?
options: It must have the same potential difference across it as the resistor
A low resistance makes the needle deflect further for a given current in the circuit
It carries the whole current it measures, and its low resistance barely disturbs the circuit
Connecting it in series protects it from the full supply voltage
questions.why: Why C is right: An ammeter measures the current passing through it, so it has to lie in the path of that current. Any resistance it adds changes what it is trying to measure, so it is made as small as possible. Why the others are wrong: A describes a parallel connection, which is how a voltmeter is used · B confuses the meter's internal resistance with its sensitivity · D invents a protection argument; the reason is non-disturbance of the circuit

questions.q: A student connects the voltmeter in series with the resistor instead of across it. What happens?
options: It short-circuits the supply and a very large current flows
Its very high resistance nearly stops the current, so both meters read almost nothing useful
Nothing changes, because the same current flows everywhere in a series loop
It reads the full supply voltage instead of the drop across the resistor
questions.why: Why B is right: A voltmeter is built with a very high resistance so that in parallel it draws almost no current. Placed in series, that same high resistance dominates the loop and chokes the current off. Why the others are wrong: A describes the opposite blunder — an ammeter connected across the supply · C assumes a meter is an ideal wire and ignores its internal resistance · D assumes current still flows normally, which the high resistance prevents

questions.q: Ohm's law states that:
options: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at any temperature
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature
The current through a conductor is inversely proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature
The resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant current
questions.why: Why B is right: The constant-temperature proviso is part of the law, and it is precisely the condition a hot tungsten filament violates. Why the others are wrong: A drops the constant-temperature condition, which is what makes filaments non-ohmic · C inverts the proportionality · D makes resistance the dependent variable, which is not Ohm's law

questions.q: The graph of V (in volts) against I (in milliamps) for a resistor is a straight line through the origin of slope 0.998 V/mA. What is the resistance?
questions.why: Why D is right: 1 V/mA = 1 V / 10⁻³ A = 10³ Ω = 1 kΩ. So 0.998 V/mA = 0.998 kΩ = 998 Ω. Why the others are wrong: A reports the bare number as ohms, dropping the milli- prefix entirely — a factor of 1000 · B applies the mA-to-A conversion in the wrong direction, dividing by 1000 instead of multiplying · C takes the reciprocal of the slope, as if the graph were I against V

questions.q: A student plots I against V instead of V against I. What does the slope of that graph represent?
options: The conductance, 1/R
The resistance R, exactly as before
R²
Nothing useful, because the graph is no longer a straight line
questions.why: Why A is right: With I on the vertical axis, I = (1/R)V, so the gradient is the reciprocal of the resistance. Either plot is acceptable provided you say which — but the slope must then be interpreted correctly. Why the others are wrong: B assumes swapping the axes leaves the gradient unchanged · C invents a power relation where the reciprocal is required · D a proportional relation stays linear whichever variable is plotted first

questions.q: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
questions.why: Why C is right: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/30 = 6/60 + 3/60 + 2/60 = 11/60, so R = 60/11 = 5.45 Ω — smaller than the smallest branch, as it must be. Why the others are wrong: A stops at 1/R = 11/60 = 0.183 and never takes the reciprocal · B adds the resistances, which is the series rule · D takes the arithmetic mean of the three values

questions.q: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are combined. What are the equivalent resistances in series and in parallel respectively?
options: 9 Ω and 4.5 Ω
9 Ω and 0.5 Ω
9 Ω and 2 Ω
2 Ω and 9 Ω
questions.why: Why C is right: Series: 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. Parallel: R = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 18/9 = 2 Ω, which is smaller than the 3 Ω branch, as required. Why the others are wrong: A averages the two resistors for the parallel case instead of combining reciprocals · B computes 1/6 + 1/3 = 0.5 and never inverts the result · D interchanges the series and parallel results

questions.q: Why is it significant that the V against I line for an ohmic resistor passes through the origin?
options: Because a line through the origin is the only kind whose gradient can be read with a ruler
Because an ohmic conductor gives no p.d. at zero current, so a non-zero intercept signals a fault
Because a resistance read off the graph would otherwise come out negative at low currents
Because the power supply is switched on from 0 V, so the first reading must lie at the origin
questions.why: Why B is right: The zero intercept is part of the claim being tested, not a decoration: a line that misses the origin points to a systematic fault such as a meter zero offset. That is why the origin is deliberately included on the axes for this experiment. Why the others are wrong: A passing through the origin and being straight are separate properties, and neither controls how a gradient is read · C the sign of R is not what the intercept tests · D confuses the starting point of the procedure with a property of the conductor ### Section D — Non-ohmic conduction and Joule's law (Week 3)

questions.q: A conducting device obeys Ohm's law if:
options: Its resistance is independent of temperature
It conducts equally well in both directions, even though its resistance varies with the applied voltage
It dissipates power according to P = I²R
The resistance between any pair of points is independent of the magnitude and polarity of the applied p.d.
questions.why: Why D is right: That is the careful statement the course gives. Both conditions matter: the resistance must not change when the voltage is raised, and it must not change when the voltage is reversed. Why the others are wrong: A states a material property; the law concerns dependence on the applied p.d. · B keeps polarity independence but abandons magnitude independence, which is exactly what a filament violates · C P = I²R holds for every conductor, ohmic or not, so it cannot be the test

questions.q: At one operating point a tungsten filament carries 2.90 A and has resistance 5.17 Ω. What power is dissipated as heat?
questions.why: Why A is right: P = I²R = (2.90)² × 5.17 = 8.41 × 5.17 = 43.5 W. As a check, P = VI with V = IR = 15.0 V gives 15.0 × 2.90 = 43.5 W. Why the others are wrong: B computes IR rather than I²R, forgetting to square the current · C squares after multiplying, evaluating (IR)² instead of I²R · D divides I² by R instead of multiplying

questions.q: Why does the filament of a lamp stop obeying Ohm's law as the applied voltage is raised?
options: Joule heating raises its temperature, and a metal's resistance rises with temperature, so R is not constant
Tungsten is a semiconductor, so its resistance falls sharply as the filament heats up and glows
The power supply cannot deliver enough current at high voltage, so the current levels off
At high voltage the filament begins to emit light, and the emitted energy consumes current
questions.why: Why A is right: The chain is: current meets resistance, resistance dissipates heat at I²R, temperature rises, a metal's resistance rises with temperature, so the I–V relation bends. Ohm's law's constant-temperature condition has been violated. Why the others are wrong: B tungsten is a metal and its resistance rises, not falls, with temperature · C blames the instrument for a property of the conductor · D invents a mechanism; the light is a consequence of the heating, not a cause of the bending

questions.q: A graph of I against V is drawn for a tungsten filament over the range 0.1 V to 50 V. What is its shape?
options: A straight line through the origin
It starts steeply from the origin and bends over towards the voltage axis
It starts shallow and curves upwards, away from the voltage axis
A straight line that does not pass through the origin
questions.why: Why B is right: As V rises the filament gets hotter and its resistance rises, so each extra volt buys progressively less current. The curve still passes through the origin — no voltage, no current. Why the others are wrong: A describes an ohmic resistor, which is the control case rather than the result · C would mean the resistance falls as the filament heats, the opposite of a metal's behaviour · D confuses non-ohmic behaviour with a zero-offset systematic error

questions.q: Why is tungsten chosen for lamp filaments and heating elements?
options: It is the only metal that is non-ohmic
Its resistance falls as it heats, so it draws more current and glows brighter
It has the lowest resistivity of any metal, so it wastes the least energy as heat
It withstands very high temperatures and its resistance rise is reproducible
questions.why: Why D is right: Any metal goes non-ohmic if driven hard enough; tungsten is used because it withstands the temperature without failing. Why the others are wrong: A every metal becomes non-ohmic when self-heated; tungsten is not special in that respect · B reverses the temperature dependence of a metal · C silver and copper have lower resistivity, and low resistivity is not what a filament needs

questions.q: Which of the following behaves as an ohmic conductor?
options: A thermistor used in a temperature-sensing circuit
A semiconductor diode in a rectifier circuit
A metal-film resistor held at constant temperature
A light-dependent resistor in a street-lamp switch
questions.why: Why C is right: Kept at constant temperature, a metal-film resistor has a fixed V/I ratio regardless of the size or polarity of the applied p.d. Why the others are wrong: A a semiconductor device whose resistance changes drastically with temperature — the standard non-ohmic example · B has very high resistance one way and very low the other, so its resistance depends on polarity · D its resistance is set by the illumination, so V/I is not a fixed constant

questions.q: For a tungsten filament driven over the full range 0.1 V to 50 V, P = VI is computed and plotted against I². The graph is:
options: An exact straight line, because P = I²R holds at every point
A curve of decreasing gradient, because the current saturates at high voltage
A curve of increasing gradient, because the gradient equals R and R rises as the filament heats
A straight line that misses the origin
questions.why: Why C is right: The gradient of P against I² is the resistance. Since the whole point of the week is that R rises by roughly a factor of nine over this range, the plot must steepen — it cannot be a single straight line. Why the others are wrong: A P = I²R is always true, but it only plots straight where R is constant, which is what is being disproved · B would require the resistance to fall as the filament heats · D at zero current no power is dissipated, so the plot must start at the origin ### Section E — Kirchhoff's current law (Week 4)

questions.q: Kirchhoff's Current Law states that the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. On which conservation principle does it rest?
options: Conservation of energy
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of magnetic flux
Conservation of charge
questions.why: Why D is right: A junction is a point and cannot store charge, so whatever flows in must flow out at the same instant. Why the others are wrong: A that is the basis of the voltage law, not the current law — the commonest confusion of the pair · B has no role in circuit analysis · C belongs to induction, not to currents at a node

questions.q: At a junction, currents of 0.40 A and 0.57 A flow in along wires 1 and 2, and a single current flows out along wire 3. What is the current in wire 3?
questions.why: Why A is right: By KCL the current leaving equals the sum of the currents entering: 0.40 + 0.57 = 0.97 A. Why the others are wrong: B subtracts one entering current from the other instead of adding them · C averages the two entering currents · D multiplies the two currents, which has no physical meaning here

questions.q: In the Kirchhoff experiment one branch current is recorded as I₂ = −0.416 mA. What does the minus sign mean?
options: The ammeter was connected the wrong way round, so the value should be recorded as +0.416 mA
That branch's current actually flows opposite to the direction assumed when the equations were written
Charge is being lost at that node
That branch contains the larger of the two emfs
questions.why: Why B is right: The sign is information, not an error. KCL is stated as an algebraic sum precisely so that a wrongly assumed direction corrects itself automatically. Why the others are wrong: A discards real information; dropping the sign makes the equations unsolvable · C charge conservation is never violated; a node cannot store or destroy charge · D the sign records direction of flow, not which supply is larger

questions.q: The apparatus for the Kirchhoff's laws experiment consists of a breadboard, connection cables and:
options: One DC power supply, three variable resistors and two ammeters
Two DC power supplies, five variable resistors and three voltmeters
One DC power supply, five variable resistors, one ammeter and one voltmeter
Two DC power supplies, five variable resistors and three ammeters
questions.why: Why D is right: The circuit has two emfs, five resistors R₁ to R₅ arranged in three branches, and one ammeter per branch. Why the others are wrong: A under-counts every item; the circuit needs two independent emfs · B substitutes voltmeters for the ammeters that measure the three branch currents · C a single emf cannot produce the two-loop circuit the experiment analyses

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the recording procedure in the Kirchhoff experiment?
options: Both supplies are set to a maximum of 9 V and the five resistances are stepped in turn while the emfs stay fixed
A single supply is stepped in 1 V intervals while the resistances are held fixed
Both supplies are set to a 50 V maximum, the emfs are then adjusted, and readings taken at 3 V intervals
The emfs are held fixed while each of the five resistors is varied in turn
questions.why: Why C is right: The 50 V button sets the range; the dial then sets the working emf, which is stepped in regular 3 V intervals with all three ammeter readings captured at each step. Why the others are wrong: A confuses the working emf with the range setting, and varies the wrong quantity · B the circuit uses two supplies, and the step is 3 V · D the resistances are fixed for a run; it is the emf that is stepped

questions.q: For one branch the calculated current is 0.4783 mA and the measured current is 0.479 mA. Taking the calculated value as the reference, what is the percentage difference?
questions.why: Why B is right: % difference = [(observed − reference)/reference] × 100 = [(0.479 − 0.4783)/0.4783] × 100 = +0.146 %, i.e. +0.15 %. The positive sign says the observed value is the higher of the two. Why the others are wrong: A interchanges observed and reference in the numerator and denominator · C omits the multiplication by 100 and then labels the fraction a percentage · D quotes the absolute difference in milliamps as though it were a percentage ### Section F — Kirchhoff's voltage law (Week 5)

questions.q: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that around any closed loop the sum of the voltage drops equals the sum of the emfs. On which conservation principle does it rest?
options: Conservation of energy
Conservation of charge
Conservation of magnetic flux
Conservation of power in each branch
questions.why: Why A is right: Potential is energy per unit charge. Carry a unit charge once round a loop and it returns to the same potential, so every joule the battery supplies is given back to the resistors. Why the others are wrong: B that is the basis of the current law; the material itself confuses the two, and the confusion costs marks · C belongs to electromagnetic induction, not to a DC loop · D power is not a conserved quantity that can be summed round a loop

questions.q: Using the sign convention stated in the course, the potential difference across a resistor is taken as positive when the resistor is traversed:
options: In the direction opposite to the current through it
In the same direction as the current through it
In the direction of increasing resistance around the loop
In either direction, since the drop across a resistor is always positive
questions.why: Why B is right: Traverse with the current and the p.d. is positive; traverse against it and the p.d. is negative. Fix every current direction before starting and apply the rule mechanically. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the stated convention and flips the sign of every resistor term · C invents a rule based on resistor values rather than current direction · D abandons the algebraic sign, which is what makes the loop equations solvable

questions.q: A 12 V battery drives current through two resistors in series. The potential difference across the first resistor is 5 V. What is the potential difference across the second?
options: 7 V
questions.why: Why A is right: By KVL the drops round the loop must add up to the emf: 5 + V₂ = 12, so V₂ = 7 V. Why the others are wrong: B adds the emf and the first drop instead of subtracting · C assumes the full emf appears across each resistor, which is the parallel case · D divides the emf by the first drop, which has no physical meaning

questions.q: After eliminating I₃, the loop equations for one row of the Kirchhoff data reduce to 14.5 I₁ + 9.5 I₂ = 9 and 11 I₂ − 5 I₁ = −9, with currents in mA. What is I₁?
questions.why: Why C is right: From the second equation I₂ = (5I₁ − 9)/11. Substituting and multiplying through by 11: 159.5 I₁ + 47.5 I₁ − 85.5 = 99, so 207 I₁ = 184.5 and I₁ = 0.891 mA. Why the others are wrong: A solves correctly but quotes the magnitude of I₂ instead of I₁ · B quotes I₃ = I₁ + I₂, the answer to a different part of the question · D loses the minus sign on the right of the second equation before substituting

questions.q: Why is the Kirchhoff circuit analysis carried out in volts, milliamps and kilohms?
options: Because the ammeters read in milliamps and formulae must use the units of the instrument
Because the kilohm is the SI unit of resistance
Because the emfs are given in volts and the units must match the largest quantity
Because 1 mA × 1 kΩ = 1 V exactly, so no powers of ten enter the working at all
questions.why: Why D is right: Working consistently in V/mA/kΩ is equivalent to working in V/A/Ω; the products come out right without a single conversion. Mixing the two systems is where magnitude errors breed. Why the others are wrong: A no formula is bound to an instrument's display unit; consistency is what matters · B the SI unit is the ohm; the kilohm is a convenience here · C matching to the largest quantity is not a rule of unit consistency

questions.q: What is the correct first step in solving the three simultaneous circuit equations?
options: Use KCL to replace I₃ by I₁ + I₂, leaving two equations in two unknowns
Assume I₂ is zero because its measured value is negative
Add the two loop equations to eliminate the emfs
Solve the first loop equation for I₃ and substitute it into the KCL equation
questions.why: Why A is right: Eliminating I₃ first turns an awkward three-equation problem into a routine pair of simultaneous equations. Practising this step until it is automatic is the single best preparation for the hardest calculation in the course. Why the others are wrong: B discards a real branch current on the basis of a sign that only records direction · C the emfs are known constants; there is nothing to be gained by removing them · D leaves three unknowns still in play instead of reducing the count ### Section G — Charging a capacitor (Week 6)

questions.q: Capacitance is:
options: The charge stored per unit area of plate, measured in coulombs per square metre
The energy stored in the electric field per unit voltage across the plates, measured in coulombs
The potential difference produced per unit charge, measured in farads
The constant of proportionality between the charge stored and the p.d. across the capacitor
questions.why: Why D is right: Q = CV, with Q in coulombs, V in volts and C in farads. A capacitor is the device; capacitance is the property of the device. Why the others are wrong: A describes a surface charge density, not capacitance · B confuses stored energy with stored charge and gives the wrong unit · C inverts the definition; that ratio is 1/C

questions.q: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = εA/d. The plate separation is doubled and nothing else is changed. The capacitance:
options: Doubles
Quarters
Halves
Is unchanged, because C depends only on the dielectric
questions.why: Why C is right: C is inversely proportional to d, so doubling the separation halves the capacitance. Why the others are wrong: A reads the relation as a direct proportionality instead of an inverse one · B treats the separation as though it entered squared · D ignores both the geometry factors in the formula

questions.q: One time constant after the switch is closed on a charging capacitor, the potential difference across it has reached:
options: 36.8 % of its final value
63.2 % of its final value
50 % of its final value
100 % of its final value
questions.why: Why B is right: V(τ) = V₀(1 − e⁻¹) = V₀(1 − 0.368) = 0.632 V₀. Charging rises to 63.2 %; discharging falls to 36.8 %. Why the others are wrong: A quotes the discharging figure, e⁻¹, for a charging circuit · C assumes the time constant is a half-life, which it is not · D assumes charging is complete after one time constant

questions.q: A capacitor of 470 μF is charged through a 22 kΩ resistor. What is the time constant?
questions.why: Why B is right: τ = RC = (2.2 × 10⁴ Ω)(4.70 × 10⁻⁴ F) = 10.34 s. Both quantities must be converted to SI before multiplying. Why the others are wrong: A leaves the capacitance in microfarads, a factor of 10⁶ too large · C leaves the resistance in kilohms, a factor of 10³ too small · D computes 1/RC, taking the reciprocal at the wrong stage

questions.q: Graphical analysis of a charging curve gives τ = 9.97 s with R = 10 kΩ. What is the capacitance?
options: 997 μF
questions.why: Why C is right: C = τ/R = 9.97/(1.00 × 10⁴) = 9.97 × 10⁻⁴ F. Since 1 F = 10⁶ μF, this is 997 μF — within 0.3 % of the stated 1000 μF. Why the others are wrong: A converts farads to microfarads by dividing by 10⁶ instead of multiplying · B multiplies τ by R instead of dividing · D slips a decimal place when converting the resistance to ohms

questions.q: In an RC circuit the resistance is doubled while the capacitance is unchanged. What happens?
options: τ halves, so the capacitor reaches its final voltage twice as fast
τ is unchanged, because it depends only on the capacitance
τ is unchanged but the final voltage halves
τ doubles, so charging to any given fraction of V₀ takes twice as long
questions.why: Why D is right: A larger R throttles the current flowing onto the plates. Since τ = RC, doubling R doubles the time constant and the circuit charges more slowly. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the direct proportionality between τ and R · B drops R from τ = RC altogether · C confuses the time constant with the potential divider behaviour of a steady-state circuit

questions.q: In the charging experiment, how are the voltmeter readings taken?
options: Every 10 seconds until the reading stops rising, with at least ten readings
Every 10 seconds, stopping after exactly seven readings
Every second until the LED goes out
Only at the moments when the reading is 63.2 % and 36.8 % of maximum
questions.why: Why A is right: Regular intervals spread the points evenly along the curve, and at least ten readings make the analysis believable. Why the others are wrong: B seven is below the minimum the procedure sets for this experiment · C the LED belongs to the discharging circuit and is not a timing signal · D reduces the experiment to two points, leaving nothing to plot or average ### Section H — Discharging a capacitor (Week 7)

questions.q: Which pair of equations correctly describes the charging and the discharging of a capacitor respectively?
options: V = V₀e^(−t/τ) and V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ))
V = V₀(1 − e^(−τ/t)) and V = V₀e^(−τ/t)
V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)) and V = V₀e^(−t/τ)
V = V₀(1 + e^(−t/τ)) and V = V₀e^(+t/τ)
questions.why: Why C is right: Charging climbs from zero towards V₀; discharging falls from V₀ towards zero. Both have the same time constant τ = RC. Why the others are wrong: A interchanges the two, so the capacitor charges by falling and discharges by rising · B inverts the exponent, giving a function that is undefined at t = 0 · D loses the sign structure, so the discharge grows without limit

questions.q: In the discharging experiment, why must you wait until the voltmeter reaches its maximum before opening the switch?
options: Because V₀ is the reference for every later reading, and an incomplete charge makes every point wrong
Because the capacitor would otherwise be damaged by the sudden reversal of current
Because the LED will not light unless the capacitor is fully charged
Because the time constant depends on the initial voltage
questions.why: Why A is right: The whole analysis is expressed as a fraction of V₀. Start early and the 36.8 % line sits at the wrong height and the linearised intercept no longer recovers the supply voltage. Why the others are wrong: B invents a safety reason for what is a measurement requirement · C the LED indicates the switch state, not the state of charge · D τ = RC depends only on the components, never on V₀

questions.q: To linearise the discharge of a capacitor, what is plotted, and what are the slope and intercept?
options: ln V against t; slope = −τ, intercept = ln V₀
ln V against t; slope = −1/τ, intercept = ln V₀
ln V against ln t; slope = −1/τ
V against ln t; slope = −1/τ
questions.why: Why B is right: Taking natural logs of V = V₀e^(−t/τ) gives ln V = (−1/τ)t + ln V₀, a straight line of negative gradient. Why the others are wrong: A takes the reciprocal at the wrong stage, so τ comes out as the slope itself · C logs the time axis as well, which is the power-law rule misapplied to an exponential · D logs the wrong axis entirely, so the plot is not straight

questions.q: On a ln V against t plot for a discharging capacitor, two points on the best-fit line are (3.16 s, 2.302) and (87.59 s, −0.261). What is the time constant?
questions.why: Why D is right: slope = (−0.261 − 2.302)/(87.59 − 3.16) = −2.563/84.43 = −0.03036 s⁻¹, and τ = −1/slope = 32.9 s. Why the others are wrong: A quotes the slope itself as the time constant instead of taking its negative reciprocal · B keeps the minus sign, giving a negative time, which is impossible · C reads the run of the triangle as the time constant

questions.q: Analysis of a discharge gives C = 2193 μF for a capacitor whose stated value is 2200 μF. What is the percentage error?
questions.why: Why D is right: % error = [(2200 − 2193)/2200] × 100 = (7/2200) × 100 = 0.318 %, comfortably inside the 5 % the course accepts. Why the others are wrong: A slips a decimal place in the division · B computes the fraction and omits the multiplication by 100 · C quotes the absolute difference in microfarads as a percentage

questions.q: A student plots log₁₀ V against t for a discharging capacitor and then computes τ = −1/slope. What is wrong with the result?
options: It is about 2.30 times too small, because the base-10 slope is steeper
It is about 2.30 times too large, because with base-10 logs the slope is −1/(2.303τ)
It is unchanged, because changing the base of a logarithm only shifts the intercept
It comes out negative, because log₁₀ of a voltage below 1 V is negative
questions.why: Why B is right: Converting bases, log₁₀ V = log₁₀ V₀ − t/(2.303τ), so −1/slope returns 2.303τ rather than τ. The linearisation requires natural logs. Why the others are wrong: A gets the direction of the error backwards; the base-10 line is shallower, not steeper · C a change of base scales the whole line, altering the gradient as well as the intercept · D individual negative values do not change the sign of the gradient

questions.q: A ln V against t plot for a discharging capacitor has intercept 2.398. What was the initial voltage V₀?
questions.why: Why A is right: The intercept is ln V₀, so V₀ = e^2.398 = 11.0 V. Recovering the known supply voltage is a powerful check that model and data agree. Why the others are wrong: B reads the intercept itself as the voltage, forgetting it is a logarithm · C computes 10^2.398, using base-10 antilogs on a natural-log plot · D takes the reciprocal of the correct value ### Section I — Boyle's law (Week 8)

questions.q: Boyle's law states that:
options: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed quantity of gas is directly proportional to its temperature
At constant volume, the pressure of a fixed quantity of gas is directly proportional to its temperature
At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed quantity of gas is inversely proportional to its volume
At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed quantity of gas is directly proportional to its volume
questions.why: Why C is right: PV = constant, so P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. The constant-temperature condition and the fixed quantity of gas are both part of the law. Why the others are wrong: A states Charles's law · B states Gay-Lussac's law · D makes the proportionality direct instead of inverse

questions.q: Why does the apparatus for the Boyle's law experiment include a thermometer?
options: To supply the temperature needed in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT for the trapped sample
To confirm that the temperature stays constant, the condition under which the law holds
To correct the density of the mercury for thermal expansion
To measure the temperature rise caused by compressing the trapped air
questions.why: Why B is right: The thermometer's only job is to verify a condition of the law. No temperature value enters the calculation at all. Why the others are wrong: A the analysis uses PV = constant; no absolute temperature is substituted anywhere · C ρ is taken as 13 600 kg/m³ throughout; no expansion correction is made · D if the air warmed on compression the law would not apply; the point is that it does not

questions.q: In the J-tube experiment, why does raising the open arm increase the pressure on the trapped air?
options: The trapped volume falls, and pressure rises because volume falls
Raising the arm seals the closed end more tightly, so a larger quantity of air is trapped
The atmospheric pressure acting on the open arm increases with height
The extra mercury column of height h adds ρgh to the atmospheric pressure already present
questions.why: Why D is right: P_f = Pₐ + ρgh. Before the arm is raised the levels are equal, so the trapped air sits at atmospheric pressure; raising the arm adds the hydrostatic term. Why the others are wrong: A reverses cause and effect: the compression is the consequence, not the mechanism · B the quantity of trapped gas is fixed throughout; nothing is added · C atmospheric pressure falls very slightly with height and is treated as constant here

questions.q: Mercury of density 13 600 kg/m³ stands 0.10 m higher in the open arm than in the closed arm. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and atmospheric pressure as 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, what is the pressure of the trapped air?
questions.why: Why C is right: ρgh = 13 600 × 9.8 × 0.10 = 1.333 × 10⁴ Pa, and P_f = Pₐ + ρgh = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 1.333 × 10⁴ = 1.146 × 10⁵ Pa. Why the others are wrong: A gives the hydrostatic term alone and forgets to add atmospheric pressure · B leaves h in centimetres, making ρgh a hundred times too large · D subtracts ρgh from atmospheric pressure instead of adding it

questions.q: Which graph verifies Boyle's law, and what does its slope represent?
options: 1/V against P — a straight line through the origin of slope 1/(P₀V₀)
P against V — a straight line of slope −P₀V₀
1/V against P — a straight line through the origin of slope P₀V₀
V against P — a straight line through the origin of slope 1/(P₀V₀)
questions.why: Why A is right: P = (P₀V₀)(1/V), so 1/V = P/(P₀V₀). Plotting the reciprocal of the volume against pressure straightens a hyperbola into a line whose gradient is the reciprocal of the constant. Why the others are wrong: B P against V is a hyperbola, not a straight line; that is exactly why the reciprocal is taken · C inverts the slope; the gradient is the reciprocal of the constant, not the constant · D plots the volume itself rather than its reciprocal, so the plot curves

questions.q: A trapped gas occupies 20.00 ml at 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. What volume does it occupy when the pressure is raised to 1.2129 × 10⁵ Pa at the same temperature?
questions.why: Why A is right: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = (1.013 × 10⁵ × 20.00)/(1.2129 × 10⁵) = 16.70 ml. Raising the pressure must reduce the volume. Why the others are wrong: B inverts the pressure ratio, so the gas expands when it is compressed · C assumes the volume is unchanged because the quantity of gas is fixed, confusing fixed mass with fixed volume · D loses a power of ten in the division

questions.q: Given that 76 cmHg = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, what is 57 cmHg in pascals?
questions.why: Why C is right: (57/76) × 1.013 × 10⁵ = 0.750 × 1.013 × 10⁵ = 7.60 × 10⁴ Pa. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the ratio, using 76/57 instead of 57/76 · B treats the cmHg reading as though it were already in pascals · D gets the ratio right but loses two powers of ten in the multiplication ### Section J — Specific heat of a solid by mixtures (Week 9)

questions.q: The specific heat capacity of a material is:
options: The heat energy needed to raise the whole body by 1 °C, measured in J/°C
The heat energy needed to raise 1 kg of it by 1 °C, measured in J/kg
The temperature rise produced by 1 J of heat, measured in °C/J
The heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 °C, measured in J/kg·°C
questions.why: Why D is right: Q = mc(Tf − Ti). Specific heat is a property of the material, defined per unit mass and per degree. Why the others are wrong: A defines heat capacity, which depends on how much material is present · B gives the right quantity with the temperature unit missing from the denominator · C inverts the definition and its unit

questions.q: What happens to the calculated specific heat of the solid if the term mc·cc for the calorimeter is left out of the mixture equation?
options: It comes out too large, because less heat is then attributed to the water in the cup
It comes out too small, because the heat that warmed the cup is not credited to the solid
It is unchanged, because the calorimeter stays at the same temperature throughout
The sign of Q reverses, so the solid appears to gain heat
questions.why: Why B is right: The cup is itself a lump of metal in thermal contact with the water and warms with it. Omitting its water equivalent understates the heat gained, so the solid appears to have released less heat than it did. Why the others are wrong: A gets the direction wrong; dropping a positive term on the gain side lowers the result · C the calorimeter starts at Tr and ends at Tf like the water · D omitting one positive term cannot reverse the direction of heat flow

questions.q: Why is the digital balance tared after the empty calorimeter has been weighed?
options: To correct for the buoyancy of the surrounding air
To convert the reading from grams to kilograms
So that the next reading gives the mass of the water alone
So that the block's mass can be read without removing the water
questions.why: Why C is right: Taring zeroes the display with the calorimeter still on the pan, so what is read after filling is mw and not mw + mc. Why the others are wrong: A a refinement far below the precision of this experiment and not part of the procedure · B taring changes the zero, never the unit; conversion is done in the analysis · D the block is weighed first, before any water is added

questions.q: A calorimeter of mass 0.03636 kg (cc = 387 J/kg·°C) holds 0.06863 kg of water (cw = 4186 J/kg·°C). The mixture's temperature rises from 16.1 °C to 17.0 °C. How much heat is gained?
questions.why: Why B is right: mw·cw = 0.06863 × 4186 = 287.29 J/°C and mc·cc = 0.03636 × 387 = 14.07 J/°C, giving 301.36 J/°C. Heat gained = 301.36 × (17.0 − 16.1) = 301.36 × 0.9 = 271 J. Why the others are wrong: A omits the calorimeter term, using the water alone · C computes the combined heat capacity in J/°C and forgets to multiply by the 0.9 °C rise · D leaves the masses in grams while the specific heats are per kilogram

questions.q: In the same experiment a solid of mass 0.0089 kg cools from 91.3 °C to 17.0 °C and gives up 271 J. What is its specific heat capacity?
options: 410 J/kg·°C
391 J/kg·°C
questions.why: Why A is right: ms·cs(Ts − Tf) = 271 J, so cs = 271/(0.0089 × 74.3) = 271/0.6613 = 410 J/kg·°C. Why the others are wrong: B follows from omitting the calorimeter term when computing the heat gained · C leaves the solid's mass in grams, a factor of 1000 · D uses the water's 0.9 °C rise in place of the solid's 74.3 °C fall

questions.q: The experiment gives 410 J/kg·°C for copper, whose accepted value is 387 J/kg·°C. What is the percentage error?
questions.why: Why D is right: % error = |(387 − 410)/387| × 100 = (23/387) × 100 = 5.9 %. The denominator is the accepted value. Why the others are wrong: A divides by the experimental 410 instead of the accepted 387 · B quotes the absolute difference in J/kg·°C as though it were a percentage · C computes the fraction and omits the multiplication by 100

questions.q: In this run the mixture warms from 16.1 °C to only 17.0 °C. Which is the strongest comment on the result?
options: The mass of the solid is the smallest quantity measured, so it dominates the uncertainty
The accepted value of cw is quoted to only four figures, which limits the result
The thermometer's absolute calibration is critical, since absolute temperatures are used
The 0.9 °C rise carries about 11 % uncertainty; use a larger block or less water
questions.why: Why D is right: The weakest measurement dominates the result. Naming that measurement and prescribing a fix scores far better than a general instruction to be careful. Why the others are wrong: A the balance resolves 8.9 g to far better than 11 %; smallness alone does not make a measurement uncertain · B 4186 J/kg·°C is known far more precisely than anything else in the experiment · C only temperature differences appear, so a constant calibration offset cancels ### Section K — Magnetic moment of a bar magnet (Week 10)

questions.q: A magnetic needle sits in the Earth's horizontal field H₀ and an applied field H at right angles to it. The tangent law states that:
options: H = H₀ tan θ
H = H₀ sin θ
H = H₀ / tan θ
H = H₀ cos θ
questions.why: Why A is right: The needle settles along the resultant of the two perpendicular fields, so the tangent of the deflection angle is the ratio of the applied field to the Earth's field. Why the others are wrong: B would follow if the needle aligned with a component rather than the resultant · C inverts the relation, so a larger applied field would give a smaller deflection · D uses the wrong trigonometric ratio, giving a non-zero field at zero deflection

questions.q: A tangent galvanometer consists of:
options: A coil suspended between the poles of a permanent magnet, carrying a light pointer
A pivoted compass needle at the centre of a circular coil, over an angular scale
A soft-iron vane pulled into a fixed coil against a spring
A bar magnet suspended by a torsion fibre above a scale
questions.why: Why B is right: The needle is free to rotate and rests along magnetic north when undisturbed; that alignment is the reference from which all deflections are measured. Why the others are wrong: A describes a moving-coil galvanometer, a different instrument · C describes a moving-iron meter, which has no compass needle and no tangent law · D describes a magnetometer of a different type; there is no coil and no pivoted needle

questions.q: At each distance, eight deflection angles are recorded and averaged. What is the main purpose of taking eight rather than simply repeating one reading eight times?
options: Averaging eight readings reduces the random error by a factor of eight
The deflection drifts with time, so several readings are needed to extrapolate back
The eight readings are taken in configurations that cancel systematic errors
The Earth's field varies during the experiment and the average compensates for it
questions.why: Why C is right: Reading both ends of the needle cancels an off-centre pivot; reversing the polarity cancels a misaligned scale zero; repeating on the other side of the rule cancels an error in the assumed position of the magnet or the galvanometer. Why the others are wrong: A averaging reduces random error, but not by the number of readings, and that is not why these eight configurations are used · B the deflection is steady once the needle settles; nothing is extrapolated · D H₀ is treated as constant throughout; it is the apparatus, not the field, that is being corrected

questions.q: What specific error is removed by reversing the magnet's polarity and re-recording?
options: The random scatter in reading the needle against the scale
A fixed misalignment of the scale's zero relative to the magnet's north–south line
The demagnetising of the bar during the experiment, by averaging its pole strength
The error caused by the magnet not lying exactly along the rule's axis
questions.why: Why B is right: Reversing flips the direction of the magnet's field. A fixed angular offset then adds to one pair of readings and subtracts from the other, so the mean of all four is free of it. Why the others are wrong: A scatter is reduced by repetition, not specifically by reversal · C reversing the orientation does not alter the magnet's pole strength · D that is removed by repeating on the other side of the rule, not by reversing polarity

questions.q: At one distance the eight recorded angles are 32°, 32°, 30°, 30°, 32°, 32°, 31° and 31°. What is θ_AV?
questions.why: Why A is right: The sum is 250°, and 250/8 = 31.25°. The angles are averaged first, and the tangent is taken afterwards. Why the others are wrong: B averages only the first pair of angles and ignores the other six · C divides the sum by four instead of eight · D quotes the sum and never divides at all

questions.q: For a bar magnet of half-length L = 0.05 m observed end-on at d = 0.45 m, what is the value of d/(d² − L²)²?
questions.why: Why D is right: d² − L² = 0.2025 − 0.0025 = 0.2000 m², so (d² − L²)² = 0.04000 m⁴ and d/(d² − L²)² = 0.45/0.04000 = 11.25 m⁻³. Why the others are wrong: A puts d² in the numerator instead of d, giving 0.2025/0.04000 · B forgets to square the bracket, dividing by 0.2000 instead of 0.04000 · C takes the reciprocal of the correct value

questions.q: Why does the analysis average the eight angles and then take the tangent, rather than taking eight tangents and averaging those?
options: Because averaging tangents would give a result with the wrong units
Because it is tan θ that appears in the theory, so the tangents must be averaged
Because tan is non-linear: the tangent of the mean is not the mean of the tangents
Because either route gives the same answer, and averaging angles is simply quicker
questions.why: Why C is right: Averaging is a linear operation and tan is not, so the two routes give different numbers. The course specifies averaging the angles. Why the others are wrong: A both routes give a dimensionless number; units are not the issue · B states the opposite of the course's instruction while sounding plausible · D assumes averaging commutes with a non-linear function, which is exactly the error

questions.q: A bar magnet 10 cm long is found to have a magnetic dipole moment of 4.86 A·m². What is its pole strength?
questions.why: Why C is right: M = 2mL, where 2L is the magnet's full length, so m = M/0.10 = 48.6 A·m. The moment is in A·m²; the pole strength is in A·m. Why the others are wrong: A divides by the half-length 0.05 m instead of the full length 0.10 m · B leaves the length in centimetres, dividing by 10 instead of 0.10 · D quotes the dipole moment again, confusing pole strength with magnetic moment ### Section L — Permeability of free space (Week 11)

questions.q: What did Hans Christian Ørsted discover in 1820?
options: A current is induced in a coil when a magnet is moved through it
Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other
A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences a force at right angles to its velocity
A compass needle near a current-carrying conductor is deflected, the deflection increasing with the current
questions.why: Why D is right: That observation linked electricity to magnetism and founded electromagnetism. Why the others are wrong: A describes Faraday's law of induction, discovered later and by someone else · B is Ampère's force law, a later consequence rather than Ørsted's observation · C states the magnetic force on a moving charge, not the deflection of a compass by a current

questions.q: In this experiment the movable magnetic probe and the tesla meter together:
options: Measure the current flowing in the loop
Measure the flux density B at a chosen distance z along the axis of the coil
Measure the radius R of the circular loop
Measure the permeability directly, so that no graph is needed
questions.why: Why B is right: The probe slides along the axis with its position z read on a scale; the tesla meter displays the flux density at that position. Why the others are wrong: A that is the ammeter's job; the probe reads a field, not a current · C R is selected when the coil is chosen, not measured by the probe · D μ₀ is obtained as the slope of a graph; no instrument reads it off

questions.q: A single circular loop of radius 0.10 m carries a current of 1.0 A. What is the flux density at the centre of the loop?
questions.why: Why A is right: At z = 0 the axial formula reduces to B = μ₀I/(2R) = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1.0)/(2 × 0.10) = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶/0.20 = 6.28 × 10⁻⁶ T, which is 6283 nT. Why the others are wrong: B omits the factor of 2 in the denominator, using μ₀I/R · C leaves the radius in centimetres, so 2R is taken as 20 instead of 0.20 · D substitutes μ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ in place of μ₀ itself

questions.q: What should be plotted so that the permeability of free space appears directly as a slope?
options: B against IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)]; the slope is μ₀ and the intercept zero
IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)] against B; the slope is μ₀ and the intercept zero
B against (R² + z²)^(3/2); the slope is μ₀IR²/2
B against z; the slope is μ₀
questions.why: Why A is right: Writing B = μ₀ × {IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)]} matches y = mx + c with the whole geometric factor as x, so the gradient is the constant itself and no further arithmetic is needed. Why the others are wrong: B interchanges the axes, so the gradient is 1/μ₀ rather than μ₀ · C B is inversely proportional to that quantity, so the plot is a curve · D B falls non-linearly with z, so this plot is not a straight line at all

questions.q: For a loop of radius R = 0.10 m carrying I = 1.0 A, what is the value of IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)] at z = 0.10 m?
questions.why: Why B is right: R² + z² = 0.0100 + 0.0100 = 0.0200 m², and (0.0200)^(3/2) = 0.0200 × 0.14142 = 2.828 × 10⁻³. So the factor is 0.0100/(2 × 2.828 × 10⁻³) = 1.77 A/m. Why the others are wrong: A is the value at z = 0; the axial distance has been left out of the bracket · C multiplies the bracket by 3/2 instead of raising it to the power 3/2 · D leaves z in centimetres, so the bracket is dominated by z² = 100

questions.q: A student computes the slope of B against the geometric factor while leaving B in nanotesla. What is the effect?
options: The slope is wrong by a factor of 10³
The slope is wrong by a factor of 10⁶
The slope comes out near 1.26 × 10³ instead of 1.26 × 10⁻⁶, wrong by a factor of 10⁹
The slope is unaffected, because both axes are scaled by the same factor
questions.why: Why C is right: 1 nT = 10⁻⁹ T, so leaving the vertical axis in nanotesla scales the whole gradient by 10⁹. Converting before plotting is not optional. Why the others are wrong: A uses the prefix for milli- rather than nano- · B uses the prefix for micro- rather than nano- · D only the vertical axis carries the nanotesla; the geometric factor is already in SI

questions.q: The accepted value of the permeability of free space is:
options: 4π × 10⁻⁷ A/m
4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A
questions.why: Why D is right: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ = 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ T·m/A. The same constant is often quoted as 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m; the two units are equivalent. Why the others are wrong: A attaches the unit of magnetic field strength to a quantity that is not a field · B quotes the permittivity of free space, ε₀, instead of the permeability · C carries an extra power of metre in the unit ### Section M — Young's modulus of a metallic beam (Week 12)

questions.q: Young's modulus is stress divided by strain. Which statement about its units is correct?
options: E is measured in N/m, because it comes from Hooke's law
Strain is measured in metres, so E is measured in N/m³
E is dimensionless, since it is the ratio of two quantities
Strain is dimensionless, so E has the units of stress, N/m² or Pa
questions.why: Why D is right: Stress is a force per unit area; strain is a ratio of two lengths and therefore carries no unit. The quotient keeps the unit of stress. Why the others are wrong: A N/m is a spring constant, not a modulus — the unit belongs to a different quantity · B treats strain as an extension rather than a ratio of extension to original length · C stress and strain are not the same kind of quantity, so their ratio is not a pure number

questions.q: In the Young's modulus experiment the dial gauge measures:
options: The thickness d of the beam
The span ℓ between the two mounts supporting the beam
The depression of the beam at its midpoint under load
The extension of the beam along its length
questions.why: Why C is right: Its plunger rests on the centre of the beam and reads the downward deflection Y directly. Why the others are wrong: A the thickness is measured beforehand with a micrometer, since it must be known very accurately · B the span is set when the mounts are placed and read from a rule · D the beam bends rather than stretching; no axial extension is measured

questions.q: A beam of span ℓ resting on two mounts carries a mass m at its centre. Given Y = mgℓ³/(48EI) and I = bd³/12 for a rectangular section, the depression is:
options: Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³)
Y = mgℓ³/(48Ebd³)
Y = mgℓ³/(192EI)
Y = mgℓ/(4Ebd³)
questions.why: Why A is right: Substituting I = bd³/12 gives Y = 12mgℓ³/(48Ebd³) = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³). Why the others are wrong: B substitutes bd³ for I without carrying the factor of 12 through the division · C uses the formula for a beam genuinely clamped at both ends, giving a depression four times too small for a beam that merely rests on two mounts · D drops the cube on the span

questions.q: What is plotted in this experiment, and what does the slope equal?
options: Y against m; a straight line of slope 4Ebd³/(gℓ³)
Y against m; a straight line through the origin of slope gℓ³/(4Ebd³)
m against Y; a straight line through the origin of slope gℓ³/(4Ebd³)
Y against m³; a straight line through the origin
questions.why: Why B is right: The depression is proportional to the load mass, so the plot is linear through the origin and its gradient carries E together with the beam's dimensions. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the gradient, so E would come out as the reciprocal of the true value · C swaps the axes but keeps the old slope expression, which then no longer matches · D invents a cube on the mass; it is the thickness that is cubed, not the load

questions.q: Two points on the best-fit line of a Y against m graph are (0.050 kg, 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m) and (0.500 kg, 5.90 × 10⁻⁴ m). What is the slope?
questions.why: Why B is right: slope = (5.90 × 10⁻⁴ − 6.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(0.500 − 0.050) = 5.30 × 10⁻⁴/0.450 = 1.18 × 10⁻³ m/kg. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the slope, dividing the run by the rise · C leaves the depression in millimetres, a factor of 10³ too large · D applies the millimetre-to-metre conversion twice

questions.q: An aluminium beam has ℓ = 1.000 m, b = 0.0300 m and d = 0.0100 m, and the Y against m graph has slope 1.18 × 10⁻³ m/kg. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is Young's modulus?
questions.why: Why C is right: E = gℓ³/(4bd³ × slope). Denominator: 4 × 0.0300 × (0.0100)³ × 1.18 × 10⁻³ = 4 × 0.0300 × 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.18 × 10⁻³ = 1.416 × 10⁻¹⁰. E = 9.8/(1.416 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.92 × 10¹⁰ Pa, or 69.2 GPa. Why the others are wrong: A uses d instead of d³, losing a factor of 10⁴ · B leaves the breadth in millimetres, using 30 instead of 0.0300 · D places the slope in the numerator instead of the denominator

questions.q: Why is the thickness of the beam the most critical of the three dimensions to measure accurately?
options: Because it enters as d³, so a 1 % error in the thickness becomes a 3 % error in E
Because the dial gauge cannot resolve the thickness accurately
Because it is the smallest dimension, so the measuring instrument is least precise on it
Because the thickness determines the mass of the beam, which adds to the load
questions.why: Why A is right: Fractional errors are multiplied by the power to which a quantity is raised. Span also enters cubed but is far larger and therefore easier to measure to a small fraction; the thickness is small and cubed at once. Why the others are wrong: B the dial gauge reads the depression; the thickness is measured with a micrometer · C a micrometer is more precise on small lengths, not less; the reason is the cube, not the size · D the beam's own weight does not appear anywhere in the working formula

questions.q: Why is the depression plotted against the load in kilograms rather than against the load's weight in newtons?
options: Because a graph must always be drawn with SI base units, and the newton is derived
Because the weight varies with location whereas the mass does not
Because the dial gauge reads mass rather than force
Because the working formula already contains g, so the slope is gℓ³/(4Ebd³)
questions.why: Why D is right: Either choice is defensible provided it is consistent. The course plots Y against m in kilograms, so g stays in the slope and in the formula used to extract E. Why the others are wrong: A graphs are routinely drawn with derived units; there is no such rule · B true of weight in general, but irrelevant in a single laboratory where g is fixed · C the dial gauge reads a depression; the masses are known from the set of slotted weights
